intro: Between the Fifth Symphony’s scherzo and finale, Mahler writes for strings and harp alone. Follow the long phrases through their swells, withdrawals and return.
question: How does a slow melody sustain tension across long phrases?

sections.label: A′ · Return
sections.mNote: opening melody and harp return, leading towards a larger swell

sections.label: Climax
sections.mNote: familiar phrase enlarged through high register and delayed resolutions

relations.label: The opening song returns
relations.basis: The Adagietto’s A–B–A′ outline restores the F-major opening after the contrasting middle span. The later excerpt lies just after the return marked near 415 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.933, sustained 15.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 413 s (cache/form/mahler-5-adagietto.txt, candidate 2; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Fourth of five movements
cues.text: The Adagietto stands between the Fifth Symphony’s scherzo and finale. Its forces are strings and harp: the winds, brass and percussion of the surrounding movements are absent.
cues.evidence: The score specifies the movement order and forces; the Mahler Foundation’s movement account describes the reduced scoring. This note concerns the whole movement.

cues.title: A line above harmony
cues.text: Across the opening, follow the long melodic phrase above the changing harmony. The slow pace makes the connection between sustained notes as important as each fresh attack.
cues.evidence: This is a listening suggestion based on the score’s slow opening. The recording rises from its low opening level around 0:05–0:10; no individual instrument entrance is claimed.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Leaning notes
cues.text: Throughout the movement, listen for notes that initially clash with the harmony and then move by step towards a chord tone. These appoggiaturas delay the point of rest inside a phrase.
cues.evidence: Appoggiaturas are a feature of the written melodic line. This general listening point does not identify a particular note at 1:20.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A letter without words?
cues.text: The conductor Willem Mengelberg wrote in his score that the Adagietto was Mahler’s declaration of love to Alma Schindler, sent to her in manuscript instead of a letter. The story rests on Mengelberg’s word alone.
cues.evidence: Mengelberg’s annotation is the evidence for the story, not independent confirmation that the manuscript was sent. The account is discussed in K. Dawn Grapes’s programme note: https://fcsymphony.org/mahler-adagietto/

cues.title: A broad early swell
cues.text: In this part of the opening section, the music builds towards a broad swell and then withdraws. Compare the length of the ascent with the quieter space that follows.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises around 2:45–3:05, stays high through 3:15 and falls markedly by 3:25. The report supports the contour, not the identification of individual string parts.

cues.title: After the swell
cues.text: Through the quieter stretch, keep following the lower lines as well as the melody. A sustained bass note or a small inner movement can change the meaning of the note above it.
cues.evidence: The report places a quieter span around 3:25–3:55. The invitation to follow lower lines is general; the analysis does not separate the string voices.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Another rise in pressure
cues.text: The opening section includes another substantial swell before the middle span. Listen for the contrast between growing intensity and the long phrase lengths, rather than expecting the pulse simply to accelerate.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises around 4:00–4:30 before falling after 4:35. The analysis does not reliably measure the beat or assign an orchestral cause.

cues.title: The more flowing middle
cues.text: The middle section carries the instruction “Fließender” — more flowing — and moves beyond the opening’s F major. Compare its phrase movement with the slower opening, without expecting a completely separate tune.
cues.evidence: The score provides the marking and contrasting middle section. A strong measured change around 4:36 suggests its approximate start; this is not a bar-aligned timing.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A middle-section swell
cues.text: The middle stretch has its own rise and retreat. Follow the whole phrase across the crest rather than taking each change in intensity as a new section.
cues.evidence: The report shows a rise in relative level around 5:20–5:35 and a drop by 5:40. These measurements locate a broad swell only.

cues.title: Preparing a return
cues.text: As the middle section continues, keep the opening melody in mind. The return will recover its slow unfolding, so a familiar contour matters more than recognising each passing chord.
cues.evidence: The score’s three-part design supplies the comparison. The analysis alone cannot establish the identity of every passing harmony.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: The opening reconsidered
cues.text: In the later return, the opening material regains the foreground. Compare its long phrases with their first appearance, and listen for how another large swell grows from familiar material.
cues.evidence: The quieter span around 6:55–7:15 is compatible with the score’s return. Its start is estimated, not established by the report’s key labels.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A second public life
cues.text: Leonard Bernstein conducted the Adagietto at Robert Kennedy’s funeral Mass in New York in 1968. Luchino Visconti used it in Death in Venice in 1971. Both settings helped give the movement associations beyond its place in the symphony.
cues.evidence: The Mahler Foundation documents the funeral performance and film use: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-movement-4-adagietto-sehr-langsam/

cues.title: Slow is an instruction
cues.text: The score’s heading is “Sehr langsam” — very slow. This audio file lasts about ten minutes twenty seconds, including its opening and final decay; that duration is not a measurement of every phrase’s pace.
cues.evidence: The tempo heading is in the score. The cached analysis measures the complete file at 621.3 seconds; no historical recording comparison is inferred from it.

cues.title: The later broad crest
cues.text: The later return grows into the movement’s largest recorded swell. Listen through the extended crest before the closing withdrawal, rather than waiting for one isolated loud note.
cues.evidence: The highest five-second relative-level windows occur around 9:20–9:45. This comparison is within this recording, not a measure of orchestral dynamics or another performance.

cues.title: The closing withdrawal
cues.text: The final phrase recedes into the remaining resonance. Listen to the length of that withdrawal after the sustained crest: the disappearance of the sound is part of the ending.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls steadily from around 9:55 through 10:15. The report supports a fading passage, not a precise final note or release time.

transitions.title: The harp falls away as harmony moves
transitions.how: The opening section’s renewed swell does not lead to another settled F-major statement. Mahler moves into the G♭-major region, a semitone above the home tonic, and asks for a more flowing pace. The harp falls almost silent (it returns only briefly, in bars 45–48), leaving the strings to carry both the line and its harmonic motion. The melody retains the opening’s leaning dissonances and connected phrases; altered harmony and accompaniment, rather than a new orchestral family, distinguish the middle section.
transitions.evidence: The B boundary is 4:36, the report’s strongest novelty peak, with relative level falling after the preceding swell. The score supplies Fließender, the G♭ region and the harp’s near-absence (Peters full score, pp. 180–181: a brief return in bars 45–48); the Mahler Foundation describes the middle-section scoring at https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/symphony-no-5/symphony-no-5-movement-4-adagietto-sehr-langsam/. Machine key labels are not used as chord identifications.

transitions.title: The flowing line recovers its first breath
transitions.how: The middle section’s changing harmonies recede and the original slow phrase returns, with the harp again articulating the harmony beneath sustained strings. F major becomes the tonal goal again, but Mahler restores the melody’s suspensions as well as its notes: the line must still lean against a chord before settling. The join therefore sounds like a recovery of breathing and accompaniment, not a blunt tonic chord interrupting the middle section.
transitions.evidence: The A′ boundary is estimated at 6:55, in a quieter 6:45–7:15 stretch. The relations file matches the opening at 10.5–26 s with 423.5–439 s, provisionally supporting the return rather than fixing its first bar. The score supplies the restored opening material, slow pace and harp accompaniment.

transitions.title: Suspensions enlarge the familiar phrase
transitions.how: The return grows into a climax without introducing brass, winds or a new theme. Mahler raises the violin line and increases the weight of the divided strings while their inner parts continue to move beneath sustained melodic notes. Dissonances delay consonant arrivals, and dominant harmony keeps F major in prospect. The familiar phrase becomes larger through register, harmonic delay and crescendo; the bass’s direction matters as much as the high line’s reach.
transitions.evidence: The Climax boundary is 9:15; novelty peaks at 9:00 and 9:14 precede the highest relative-level windows around 9:20–9:45. String register, suspensions and dominant preparation are score-informed descriptions of the expanded returning phrase, not machine-separated voices or timestamped chords.

transitions.title: The delayed tonic is allowed to settle
transitions.how: After the extended crest, Mahler reduces the pressure rather than adding a separate closing tune. The line broadens and descends towards rest while C-dominant harmony finally yields to F major. Harp attacks and sustained string resonance separate clearly as the sound diminishes. The last tonic is prolonged quietly: harmonic arrival comes before the sound has disappeared, so the listener hears both resolution and the time it takes the instruments to release it.
transitions.evidence: The Close boundary is 10:00, near the 10:02 novelty peak; relative level falls from −10.8 dB at 9:55 to −41.4 dB at 10:15. The score supplies the dominant-to-F-major close and broadening; the report anchors the withdrawal, not the precise final chord or release.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 5, IV. Adagietto, full score (Peters, plate 9015)
source.locator: pp. 178–182. The brief harp return in bars 45–48 is proportioned between the 276 s middle and 415 s return anchors; timings are approximate.

timeline.note: Harp arpeggios unfold beneath sustained divided violas; cellos enter before the violin melody.
First violins sing above harp arpeggios, divided inner strings and pizzicato basses.
First violins rest while violas and cellos continue the phrase beneath the harp.
The high melody returns; second violins and violas sustain the inner harmony.
Both violin sections broaden the rising phrase as harp arpeggios spread across registers.
Second violins carry the line while first violins withdraw; harp and lower strings continue.
The more flowing middle begins with strings alone; first violins play warmly on the G string.
Harp briefly rejoins the middle-section swell with widely spaced rising figures.
The harp falls silent again; divided strings sustain the moving middle section.
Harp arpeggios restore the opening texture beneath the returning violin phrase.
High violins and rising cellos stretch the phrase above divided inner strings and harp.
Strings descend and taper; the harp leaves space before its final quiet chord.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
